newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Hanoi sets sights on more "democratic" legislature.
newsitem.headline: Hanoi sets sights on more "democratic" legislature.

text.p: Vietnam said on Thursday that it planned to give non-members of the ruling Communist Party a greater voice in the National Assembly to make the legislature a more "democratic" body.

National Assembly Office Director Vu Mao -- conceding that he was on sensitive political ground -- said the ratio of non-party lawmakers should be raised to 20 percent from about eight percent through elections to the assembly on July 20.
"We would like to see a certain ratio of non-party candidates," he told a news conference.
"The country of Vietnam is for all Vietnamese people. The National Assembly is the most powerful organ to represent the interests of the people."
Under new legislation, which will go before the assembly when its spring session opens next week, candidates for election would be free to campaign for votes on television, radio and newspapers.

"The current law stipulates that nominees may contact with voters under the organisation of the Vietnam Fatherland Front," Mao's office said in a statement. "The revised law expands the form of contact and conditions to mobilise supporters..."
The new law would also raise the ceiling on assembly deputies to 450 from 400, a change that would bolster an institution long seen as merely a rubber stamp for party decisions.

The National Assembly, which meets for just two one-month sessions a year and whose members are elected once every five years, has shown increasing signs of muscle-flexing over the past decade of reform.
At its last session, the assembly was highly critical of endemic corruption and even refused to endorse the government's choice for a junior ministerial post.
A new law aimed at stamping out corruption, along with provisions on drug abuse and paedophilia, will be considered at next month's session.
However, Mao said he was aware that the idea of raising the number of non-party deputies was sensitive and asked foreign journalists to report on his comments carefully.

Asked if the government would ever consider matching the ratio of party members in the assembly to the ratio of party members in the population as a whole -- one million for 77 million -- he appeared to draw a firm line.
"You can understand our history of struggle," he replied. "The party members are the ones who have made a great contribution."
Party members or not, candidates for election to the assembly must still clear the hurdle of approval by the Fatherland Front, a pillar of the party establishment.
Mao did not explain how, if the vote was free and fair, the government could set targets for the make-up of the assembly.

Vietnam made its opposition to multi-party democracy clear during a policy-defining party congress last year, accusing "forces hostile to socialism and national independence" of trying to sabotage the ideology of the party.

"Their usual method is to distort history, deny revolutionary achievements...demand a de-politicisation of the state apparatus, press for a pluralistic and a multi-party system with a view to stripping the party of its leadership role," it said.
